title: Japanese milk carton cakes are a genius idea that the world needs to know about
description: We’ve got all the details on where to find them, and how to eat them. There are many, many supermarket chains in Japan, but one of the most popular is Gyomu Super. content:
We’ve got all the details on where to find them, and how to eat them.

There are many, many supermarket chains in Japan, but one of the most popular is Gyomu Super. Colloquially known as “Gyo-su”, this chain is designed for gyomu, or business use, so it’s stocked with bargain bulk buys that are commonly purchased by restaurant owners, but it’s just as popular with regular customers and households looking to save money.

▼ Gyomu Super

Right now, the chain is in the spotlight on social media, thanks to a surprise product that not a lot of people know about: milk carton desserts. Gyomu Super actually sells around 10 varieties of these milk carton desserts, which pack around a kilo (2.2 pounds) of dessert into every carton. It’s a clever and compact way to serve up a big dessert, and now that a new Mitsuimo Cake has been added to the range for autumn, it was the perfect time for us to head out and try it.

Mitsuimo (literally “honey potato”) refers to sweet potatoes that become especially sweet and syrupy when cooked, with a moist and sticky texture. At first glance, you might think this carton contains Mitsuimo milk, if such a thing were to exist, but a closer look reveals this really is a cake, with the word “ケーキ” (“cake”) clearly printed on the packaging.

A cake in a carton sounds like a difficult thing to eat, but thankfully the pack comes with instructions on how to release the dessert from its packaging.

▼ First, open the entire thing up top so you can see into the carton…

▼…then tip it on its side and jiggle the dessert out onto a plate.

▼ Milk carton…

▼ …dessert!

▼ The cake slid out with a whoosh, surprising us with its presence.

▼ It was so golden and gleaming that it kind of looked like a gold bar.

Grabbing a knife, it slid through the dessert like butter, so we could easily cut a piece off and present it on a plate of its own.

After slicing, the dessert really began to resemble a cake, and when we tasted it, it had a rich sweetness and a sticky, dense texture, while being soft and jiggly at the same time. It was far more delicious than we thought it would be, with a texture like purin (Japanese pudding) but the taste of sweet potato.

Although it was tasty, the sweetness was quite strong, so it would be impossible for us to finish the whole carton as is. Thankfully, the pack comes with a few alternative ideas, like French Toast and Ice Cream Sandwiches, which both looked fantastic, but we decided to try their suggestion to use it as a spread.

Simply toast a thick slice of bread until golden brown, then spread on a layer of cream cheese and some of the Mitsuimo Cake.

▼ Since the Mitsuimo Cake is soft, it can be spread on toast like jam or butter.

This was a taste sensation. The rich sweetness of the sweet potato complemented the fresh tang of cream cheese to create a fantastic dessert-like treat. Great for breakfast or as a snack, this is something we could happily eat every day.

▼ Who knew carton cake on toast could be a thing?

The Mitsuimo Cake costs 537 yen (US$3.39), and with 7–8 servings in a pack, this was great value for money. The fact that it’s made domestically at a  factory Japan is another nice selling point.

▼ Once you’ve been initiated into the world of milk carton cakes, you’ll be keen to explore other options, like this Peach Jelly.

▼ Two quick and easy ways to serve up sweets at a gathering.

The only problem with the carton desserts is finding them. We found ours after visiting three different Gyomu Super branches, as they were so popular they’d already sold out. So if you do come across them, don’t hesitate to pick one up, so you too can fall in love with the wonders of Japan’s milk carton cakes.

title: Giant wagashi cushions will turn your home sweet home into home sweet Japanese sweets home

content:
Nitori lets you cuddle up with taiyaki, dorayaki, and more.

Japan has a lot of wise attitudes about food, and perhaps one of the most sensical of all is that dessert aesthetics are important. Sweets are a discretionary part of the diet, something eaten for enjoyment rather than nutrition, so if you can enjoy both the way they taste and the way they look, that’s double the fun.

Now Japanese housewares chain Nitori has extended that line of thinking, since if Japanese sweets look nice as food, they should look nice as part of your home’s interior decorations too, right?

That’s the logical conclusion being applied to Nitori’s Mochimochi Cushion line, with designs that apply wagashi (Japanese sweets) styling to mochimochi (“squeezably soft”) cushions. For example, at the end of a long, hard day at work or school, you could come home, plop yourself down on the couch, and curl up with the Taiyaki Mochimochi Cushion. The taiyaki, a pancake-like cake baked on a special grill into the shape of a fish with sweet red beans or other sweet fillings, is one of Japan’s most beloved wagashi varieties, and Nitori’s designers have done an amazing job recreating it in cushion form.

▼ Nitori taiyaki cushion

▼ Actual taiyaki

But there’s much more to the world of wagashi than just taiyaki, and Nitori actually has three other Japanese sweets cushions to fill your home with too (well, maybe two and a half others, depending on how you want to count one of them).

First up we have a dorayaki cushion, which draws its inspiration from the sandwiched sweet of two circular cakes with sweet red beans between.

▼ Dorayaki

▼ Dorayaki cushion

Then there’s the kuri manju cushion, modeled after a manju (steamed cake) with a chestnut (kuri) filling. Kuri manju are often oblong in shape and have the kanji character for kuri (栗) seared into the dough, and Nitori follows both design cues for its cushion.

▼ There’s an actual kuri manju in the wrapper in front of the cushion in this photo.

And last, there’s the Waffle Mochimochi Cushion.

This is what that “maybe two and a half other wagashi cushions” part was about. Waffles themselves, obviously, aren’t an indigenous part of Japanese cuisine. However, rather than being large enough to eat with a knife and fork, cooked to a light crisp, and drizzled with maple syrup. “waffles” in Japan are often smaller, softer, and folded around some sort of creamy filling.

Because of that, you could argue either way about whether or not Nitori’s waffle cushion represents Japanese dessert culture, but there’s no debating its cuteness, and it, like all of the other cushions, promises an invitingly mochimochi softness.

Nitori’s dorayaki and kuri manju cushions have been around for a while, but the taiyaki and waffle versions have just been added to the Mochimochi Cushion lineup. The taiyaki cushion is priced at 1,490 yen (US$9.40), while the others are 1,990 yen, and they’re all available through the Nitori online shop here.

title: 7-Eleven Japan now has Milk Miso Curry Ramen, but is that too much for one cup? [Taste test]

content:
A special kind of regional ramen makes its 7-Eleven instant noodle debut, with help from the makers of Sapporo Ichiban.

Nothing else has such a fundamental effect on the quality of ramen as the broth. Get the broth right, and you’re going to have at least an overall-good-tasting meal. If the broth is bad, though, it won’t matter what sort of noodles and toppings you have, since they’ll be soaked in subpar flavor.

With that in mind, 7-Eleven Japan is taking on a tough challenge with its latest instant ramen offering, since there’s a lot of complexity, and so also a lot of potential places to screw up, with the broth of the Milk Miso Curry Ramen.

This ramen didn’t come about by 7-Eleven just grabbing random things from around their kitchen and tossing them in the pot, though. Ramen with a mixed broth of miso, curry, and milk is a local specialty of Aomori Prefecture, located up at the northern tip of Japan’s main island of Honshu. This regional version hasn’t really spread to the rest of Japan, though, so 7-Eleven’s cup ramen version, which just recently went on sale, is going to be many people’s first encounter with milk miso curry ramen.

There’s an argument to be made, at the granular level, that the idea isn’t so strange. Ramen with miso-based broth has been popular for generations, and it’s a style especially loved by people in northern Japan. Ramen with a curry-based broth is less common, but not unheard of (though you’re more likely to run into curry udon noodles on restaurant menus than curry ramen). The island prefecture of Hokkaido, just north of Aomori, is known for “soup curry,” a variation with a more liquidy consistency than the thicker roux ordinarily used for Japanese curries. Some Japanese home chefs also like to add bit of milk to the pot when cooking curry or reheating leftover roux, to give it a richer flavor.

However, is 7-Eleven trying to be too clever by combining all three of those ingredients, miso, curry, and milk, in a single ramen broth? At the very least, it sounds like something that would require a delicate touch in balancing the flavors, but “delicate” isn’t usually a quality we associate with instant noodles.

In contrast to the complexity of the broth, making 7-Eleven’s Milk Miso Curry Ramen is simple. You just open the lid, fill the cup with boiling water up to the line marked on the inside of the container, wait four minutes for the contents to cook, and then stir in the broth packet.

Floating in the opaque brown broth were bean sprouts, wakame (seaweed), and ground meat. Appearance-wise, the broth looked pretty close to standard miso ramen broth, but it smelled different, with a buttery sweetness to the aroma that was wafting up as steam rose from the cup.

Using a spoon for extra classiness, our taste-testing reporter Yayoi Saginomiya took a sip of the broth, and much like with how it looks, the initial taste impression is strongly of miso. But as she went on eating, she could feel a building sensation of curry flavors coming on after the starting miso sensation.

However, Yayoi wouldn’t call any of the flavor profile’s notes “milky.” Moreso than milk, she felt like she was getting the flavor of butter. That might be because the broth uses powdered whole milk instead of liquid milk, something that’s probably unavoidable in order to meet the shelf-life expectations for instant ramen.

That’s not to say the broth is disappointing, though. Sure, in terms of flavor it may be more accurate to describe it as “miso curry butter ramen” than “milk miso curry ramen,” but it still tastes very good. With three ingredients that aren’t often combined together like this, there was a risk of a disorientating, discordant flavor as each of them tried to pull your taste buds in a different direction. 7-Eleven Japan, and their partners for this project at Sanyo Foods (makers of the Sapporo Ichiban instant ramen brand), though, have done an excellent job crafting a smooth, rich, and harmonious broth that’s miso-forward, with the curry coming on as a welcome guest and the milk helping tie everything together.

7-Eleven’s Milk Miso Curry Ramen may not be as dramatic-tasting as the concept sounds, but it is delicious, and if you’re a fan of miso ramen looking for a version of the broth with a twist to it, we highly recommended this.
